meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Myth is much more important and true than history. History is just journalism and you know how reliable that is'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Joseph Campbell everywhere, sourced nowhere. Wikiquote lists it as Disputed; the only evidence ever offered was a link to a Twitter-hosted image, now deleted.

answer.label: Not sourced to Joseph Campbell
answer.authorDates: Originator unidentified · in circulation online since at least March 2015
answer.sourceLine: No book, lecture, letter or interview has ever been produced for this sentence. Wikiquote carries it as the only entry in its Disputed section, noting that it is widely attributed to Campbell “though with no known source from Campbell’s works,” and the earliest copy located for this page is a Goodreads quote page archived on 14 March 2015 that credits Campbell and names no work at all.

source.excerpt: Myth is much more important and true than history. History is just journalism and you know how reliable that is.
trail: Wikiquote carries the line only in its Disputed section ↗, where it is the single entry on the whole page, annotated “Widely attributed to Campbell, though with no known source from Campbell’s works.”

On the Wikiquote talk page ↗ an editor proposed the line on 28 June 2019 and gave as its source nothing but a bare link to an image file on Twitter’s media server (the file now returns a 404) — an image, not a document. No other citation was ever added.

The earliest copy located for this page is a Goodreads quote page archived on 14 March 2015 ↗. It credits Joseph Campbell, files the line under tags such as “myth” and “journalism,” and attaches no book, page or date.

The Joseph Campbell Foundation ↗ has spent decades archiving his papers and recordings and publishing his uncollected articles, notes, letters and diaries as The Collected Works, with New World Library. No volume of that project has been cited as carrying this sentence.
source.excerptNote: There is no fuller passage to show. Every copy of this line found online is the line by itself — no page, no lecture date, no interviewer, no surrounding sentences.
source.rightsNote: Because no source work has been identified, no copyright status can honestly be asserted for this wording — it is not public domain merely because nobody can find where it came from. Had it ever been traced to a Campbell text, his major books from The Hero with a Thousand Faces (1949) onward are modern publications and would be in copyright, administered through his estate and the Joseph Campbell Foundation ↗.

author.heading: Who Joseph Campbell actually was
author.metaLine: 1904–1987 · American writer & professor of literature, Sarah Lawrence College
author.bio: Joseph John Campbell (26 March 1904 – 30 October 1987) was an American writer who taught literature at Sarah Lawrence College and spent his career on comparative mythology and comparative religion. The Hero with a Thousand Faces (1949) laid out the monomyth that later reshaped Hollywood screenwriting, and Myths to Live By (1972) gathered essays drawn from lectures he gave at New York’s Cooper Union Forum. He died in October 1987, months before the PBS series The Power of Myth, filmed with Bill Moyers, made him a household name — and made his name worth attaching to things.

misattribution.heading: How it became a Campbell quote
misattribution.intro: This is not a case of one author’s words being handed to another. It is a case of a sentence with no known author being handed to the most quotable mythologist of the twentieth century — and staying there because nobody checked.

items.why: Wikiquote places it in its Disputed section ↗ — the only entry there — with the note that it is widely attributed to Campbell though with no known source from Campbell’s works.

When the line was proposed for Wikiquote on 28 June 2019, the citation given ↗ was a bare link to an image file on Twitter’s media server, with nothing said about what the image showed. The file is now gone. A link to a picture is not a source.
The Goodreads entry archived in March 2015 ↗ already shows the pattern every later copy repeats: the sentence, a dash, the name, and nothing else.
The specialist site that traces contested quotations has no article on this line ↗. It has not been solved — only repeated.

misattribution.truthLine: The verdict to carry away is Wikiquote’s own: widely attributed to Campbell, with no known source from Campbell’s works ↗. Until someone produces a page, a tape or a byline, it is a sentence in search of an author.

context.heading: Why this one will not pin down
lead: Campbell’s documented writing on myth is definitional rather than combative. In The Power of Myth he defines a myth as a story about gods, then explains a god as a personification of a motivating power or value system operating in human life and in nature — the passage Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ cites at page 28 of the book. That is the register he actually works in: patient, comparative, explanatory.

The disputed line works differently. It is a ranking with a punchline attached — myth beats history, and history takes a shot on the way past. That shape travels beautifully on a graphic and badly through a footnote, which may be exactly why it has an enormous circulation and no paper trail at all. The one time someone was asked to source it ↗, what they produced was a link to an image file, since deleted.
detailsBody: What would settle this: a page number in any Campbell book, a dated lecture recording in the Foundation’s archive, or a named interviewer and publication. None of those has ever been offered, in the decade or more the line has been circulating.

Note what is not being claimed here. Nobody has shown that Campbell never said it — he lectured for decades, and a large volume of that material was still unpublished at his death. The honest position is narrower: no one has produced the source, and a quotation with no source is not yet a quotation.
context.pull: The only source ever offered for it was a link to a picture.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Joseph Campbell page lists this quote in its Disputed section — the only entry in that section — annotated "Widely attributed to Campbell, though with no known source from Campbell's works".
The Wikiquote talk page for Joseph Campbell has a section headed with this quote, proposed 28 June 2019, whose only offered source is a link to a Twitter-hosted image file (pbs.twimg.com).

A Goodreads quote page carrying this line, captured by the Wayback Machine on 14 March 2015, credits it simply to "Joseph Campbell" with tags including myth, journalism and truth-telling, and attaches no book, page or source.
A Quote Investigator site search for "history is just journalism" returns no article investigating this quotation.

Joseph Campbell lived 26 March 1904 – 30 October 1987, was an American writer and professor of literature at Sarah Lawrence College working in comparative mythology and comparative religion, and published The Hero with a Thousand Faces in 1949.

The Joseph Campbell Foundation archives Campbell's papers and recordings and publishes previously unavailable and out-of-print material as The Collected Works of Joseph Campbell, in collaboration with New World Library.

Myths to Live By by Joseph Campbell is held by the Internet Archive; the edition is Bantam Books (1973) and its essays derive from lectures given at the Cooper Union Forum in New York between 1958 and 1971.
